title: New Kilbryde Parish Church (Built 1712)
lore:
The History: Constructed just twenty paces west of the ivy-choked ruins, this modest, steep-roofed stone kirk features a stout bell-tower designed to withstand mountain squalls and a warm amber-lit sanctuary that still holds Sunday services.

Why It Took Over: By the early 1700s, the growing parish needed a weather-tight roof and a proper watch-house window overlooking the yard to deter body snatchers. Rather than risk disturbing the ancient, crowded burials beneath the ruined nave—or provoking the restless spirits rumored to guard it—the parish elders built on fresh ground right beside it. The glowing window in its side wall still acts as an unofficial beacon for anyone foolish enough to cross the kirkyard after dark.
imageAlt: The New Kilbryde parish church on a misty evening: a small stone kirk with a pointed bell-tower and a glowing amber window.

title: The Old Ruin: St. Mungo’s-on-the-Rigg (c. 1180–1560)
lore:
The History: Built in the late 12th century atop an older Pictish standing-stone mound, St. Mungo’s served as the parish kirk for four centuries. Its thick sandstone walls sheltered locals during border raids and housed the original carved stone font used to christen generations of the parish.

Why It Fell to Ruin: During the Scottish Reformation of 1560, Protestant reformers stripped the building of its Catholic altars, stained glass, and lead roof—melting the lead down for musket balls. Exposed to brutal Highland winters without a roof, the timber beams rotted and the eastern gable collapsed in the Great Gale of 1694. Locals avoided salvaging the fallen stones for their own cottages, convinced the kirk was cursed after the last parish priest vanished beneath the flagstones with the church silver.
